messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
Does completeness imply the intersection property?
M is complete, and F_n is a sequence of nonempty closed sets with F_{n+1} contained in F_n and diam F_n tending to 0, and we choose x_n in F_n for each n.
For m greater than n, both x_m and x_n lie in F_n, so d(x_m,x_n) is at most diam F_n.
Hence x_n is Cauchy because diam F_n tends to 0.
Completeness yields x in M with x_n converging to x.
For fixed n, every tail term x_m with m at least n lies in the closed set F_n.
Therefore the limit x lies in F_n, and the intersection of all F_n is nonempty.
Does the intersection property imply completeness?
We assume every sequence of nonempty closed sets with F_{n+1} contained in F_n and diameters tending to 0 has nonempty intersection.
We let x_n be a Cauchy sequence in M.
We define F_n to be the closure of the set of all terms x_k with k at least n.
Each F_n is nonempty, closed, and nested, and the diameters of F_n tend to 0 because x_n is Cauchy, so for every epsilon greater than 0, all sufficiently large closures have diameter less than epsilon.
What point does the property provide?
The property gives x in the intersection of all F_n.
For any epsilon greater than 0, we choose N with diam F_N less than epsilon, and then for every k with k at least N, d(x_k,x) is less than epsilon, so x_n converges to x.
Are both directions proved?
Is the equivalence complete?
Does this finish the proof?
